title: Threads, and how the JVM maps them to the OS
goal: By the end, you can explain what a thread is to the kernel, find any thread of a Java program from the kernel's side and back, say why a limit on tasks stops a program that starts too many threads, and say what virtual threads change and what they don't.
opening:
Picture a café at the morning rush, with one barista. She takes an order, starts the milk, then stands and watches it for a whole minute. Twelve people wait in line, and the only thing working is the machine.

The café's payments program, which records every card payment, has the same habit. Each payment waits about 120 ms for the card's bank to say yes, and a program with one line of work does nothing meanwhile. The easy fix is the café's: one barista per customer, one thread per payment. It works for a dozen. Run the program in a container that allows 64 tasks, though, and the threads stop starting. The error blames memory, while the memory sits nearly empty.

In Processes: fork, exec, wait and signals, every process did one thing at a time. In this lesson, we'll put many lines of work in one process, count a Java program's threads, hit that limit on purpose and meet virtual threads, which wait without holding a barista. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A Java program runs in a container, a boxed-off group of programs, that allows at most 64 tasks: things the kernel runs, such as processes and threads. The program starts threads in a loop, and each one waits. About how many does it start before it fails with `OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread`?
options: About 40 to 50
As many as its memory has room for
Thousands: the limit counts programs, not threads
warmup.why: The limit counts tasks, and every thread is a task. The JVM, the program that runs Java code, starts its own threads (the garbage collector, the JIT compilers and others), and they take a good part of the 64 before your code starts any. In the lab box it stopped at 42 in one run and 50 in another. Memory has nothing to do with it, despite the error's name, which is why the third option tempts people. The last option is the trap the error message itself sets: to the kernel, a thread counts the same as a process.

sections.h: Many waits at once: what a thread is to the kernel
sections.body:
Back to the café's payments program. Fifty payments arrive in the same second, and each one waits 120 ms for the card's bank to answer. With a single line of work, payment 2 starts only after payment 1 has its answer. Fifty payments take 6 seconds, and the processor sits idle for almost all of it. You want all 50 waiting at once, each on its own.

The first way is the one the last lesson built: one process per payment. `fork` a copy for each, and the kernel, the core of the operating system, runs the copies side by side. Old web servers, the programs that hand out web pages, worked like that. It's a poor fit for a Java program. Processes don't share memory. Every copy has its own heap, the memory where objects live, and its own copy of everything the program has loaded or worked out. Ten copies need about ten times the memory, and they can't share a single list or count between them.

What you want is several lines of work inside one process, all sharing its memory. In the café, that's more baristas behind one counter, sharing one fridge and one till. Each line of work needs only three things of its own. It needs a place in the code: a program counter, the address of the next instruction to run. It needs its own registers, the processor's small storage slots. And it needs its own **stack**, the piece of memory that holds each method call's local variables and the address to return to. One such line of work is a **thread**.

Linux builds threads and processes from the same part. The kernel schedules one kind of thing: it picks which one runs on each processor, and for how long. That thing is a **task**: a program counter, registers, a stack and an ID, the **TID** (thread ID). The system call `clone` (a request to the kernel) creates tasks. Its flags, settings passed with the call, say what the new task shares with the one that made it. These are the flags on every `clone` the JVM made in What a kernel does:

```text
CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM|...
```

`fork` passes none of the sharing flags, so its new task gets copies of everything and becomes a new process. A thread is a task created with flags that say "share, don't copy". `CLONE_VM` shares the memory, `CLONE_FILES` the open files and `CLONE_SIGHAND` the signal handlers, the functions that run when a signal (a short notice from the kernel) arrives. `CLONE_THREAD` puts the new task in its creator's **thread group**. A process, to the kernel, is a thread group: a set of tasks that share one memory.

That explains a field from the last lesson. A process's PID is the TID of its first task. The `Tgid` (thread group ID) line in `/proc/<pid>/status` shows that same number in every thread of the group. A signal sent with `kill <pid>` goes to the group as a whole.

The figure below is the picture for the rest of this lesson: a process is a box of shared memory with tasks in it. In the café, each barista is a task and the counter they share is the process. The JVM decides how Java's threads map onto those tasks, and there are two ways it does that. First, let's count the tasks in a real Java program.

sections.h: Counting the threads inside one Java program
sections.body:
Each task in a process shows up as a folder under `/proc/<pid>/task/`, named after its TID. Each folder has its own `status` and `stat` files, plus `comm`, which holds the thread's name. The JVM names its threads, so you can take a count by name.

This lesson's demo, `PaymentWorkers`, is a small pretend payments program. It starts two threads that would write to the ledger, the record of money moved, and mostly sleep. It starts one thread called `fraud-scorer` that pretends to check payments for signs of a stolen card, and keeps a processor busy. And it starts 1,000 virtual threads, the subject of the last section. Here are the most common names among its tasks in the lab box. (The lab box is the small Linux computer, run by Docker on your laptop, that this track's Try its use.)

```text
     13 ForkJoinPool-1-
      2 java
      2 C2 CompilerThre
      1 VM Thread
      1 VM Periodic Tas
```

The program has 36 tasks, though it starts only three ordinary threads of its own. The kernel keeps only the first 15 characters of a thread's name, so `ForkJoinPool-1-worker-11` becomes `ForkJoinPool-1-`. Most of the rest belong to the JVM. There are garbage collector threads (`GC Thread#0`, `G1 Conc#0`), which find and free objects nobody uses. There are the JIT compilers (`C2 CompilerThread0`, `C1 CompilerThread0`), which turn often-run code into fast processor instructions. The `VM Thread` runs jobs that need every Java thread paused. The `Signal Dispatcher` turns `kill -3` into a thread dump, a list of what every thread is doing. The two called `java` are the launcher thread from What a kernel does, whose TID is the PID, and `main`.

Many of these counts follow the number of processors the JVM sees. The lab box has 12, so the JVM made 12 carrier threads for virtual threads, which the last section explains. Start the same program with `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2`, a setting that makes the JVM believe there are 2 processors, and it has 25 tasks.

So a Java program is never one thread. Before your code starts a single one, it's already a few dozen tasks. Every one of them is something the kernel schedules, counts and can show you. Next, we'll find out which of them is using the processor.

try.title: Count a JVM's threads from outside
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the lab box: `docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box`. The demo is `os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l03/demo/PaymentWorkers.java`: two sleeping ledger writers, one busy fraud scorer and 1,000 virtual threads.
Run the first block. `& pid=$!` starts the program in the background and keeps its PID. Before the `uniq` line, guess which name will be the most common.
Then run the second block, which starts the same program as if the computer had 2 processors. Predict whether the task count goes up or down.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l03/demo/*.java
java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers 120 & pid=$!
sleep 3
ls /proc/$pid/task | wc -l
cat /proc/$pid/task/*/comm | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
grep Threads /proc/$pid/status
kill $pid

java -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2 -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers 120 & pid=$!
sleep 3; ls /proc/$pid/task | wc -l; kill $pid

try.expect:
```text
pid 41 running
36
     13 ForkJoinPool-1-
      2 java
      2 C2 CompilerThre
      1 VM Thread
      1 VM Periodic Tas
Threads:	36
pid 89 running
25
```

36 tasks, and 13 of them belong to the virtual-thread scheduler's pool: 12 carriers plus `ForkJoinPool-1-delayScheduler`, the pool's timer thread, which wakes the sleeping virtual threads. With `ActiveProcessorCount=2` the pool shrinks to 2 carriers and the total drops to 25. Your counts depend on how many processors your Docker setup has (`nproc` tells you), and the JIT sometimes adds a second C2 compiler thread.

sections.h: Finding the busy thread from both sides: ps and jstack
sections.body:
When a program burns processor time, the two halves of the story live in different places. The kernel knows which task is using the processor, by TID. The JVM knows what that thread is: its Java name and its stack trace, the chain of method calls it's in right now. To fix a loop that never rests, you need both, joined on something they share.

The join is easy for the threads you usually create. `Thread.ofPlatform().start(...)`, or the older `new Thread(...).start()`, ends in `pthread_create`. That's the thread-starting function of the C library, the code almost every Linux program uses to talk to the kernel. That ends in the `clone` from the first section. From then on, the Java thread and the task are one thing. The kernel schedules it, and `top` (a program that lists what uses the processor) shows its share. When it waits in `Thread.sleep` or a network read, the kernel puts that task to sleep. Java calls these **platform threads**, and the task under each one is often called an OS thread (OS is short for operating system). In the café, a platform thread is a barista who stays with one customer from order to cup.

Each platform thread also gets its own stack, and the JVM reserves the whole stack when it creates the thread. In the lab box that's about 2 MB per thread. (When creation fails, the JVM's log line says `stacksize: 2040k`.) On x86-64 Linux, the processor family in most Windows laptops, the default is 1 MB. Reserved isn't the same as used, though. The kernel sets the addresses aside at once, but hands out real memory one 4 KB page at a time, as the thread first touches it.

`jstack <pid>`, a tool that comes with Java, prints a thread dump, and every thread's first line carries its TID. Here is the busy thread of the demo program, found from both sides:

```text
$ ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu,comm | sort -k2 -nr | head -3
  145 99.7 fraud-scorer
  123  0.3 java
  140  0.2 C1 CompilerThre
$ jstack $pid | grep -A3 "nid=145 "
"fraud-scorer" #27 [145] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=5142.71ms elapsed=5.14s tid=0x0000ffffa014db90 nid=145 runnable  [0x0000ffff753aa000]
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
	at sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers.score(PaymentWorkers.java:45)
```

`ps -L` lists threads, and here they're sorted by their share of a processor (`pcpu`). Now read the dump's first line from left to right. `fraud-scorer` is the Java name. `#27` is the Java thread ID, the number `Thread.threadId()` returns. `[145]` is the TID. `cpu=` is the processor time this thread has used. `tid=0x...` is the address of the JVM's own record for the thread, not an ID the kernel knows, despite its name. `nid=145`, the native ID, is the TID again.

From JDK 18 on, `nid` is printed as a plain decimal number, so it matches `top` and `ps` as it is. (The JDK, the Java Development Kit, is the JVM plus its tools. Its versions are numbered, and 25 is the newest with long-term support.) JDK 17 and older print it in hexadecimal, base 16, as `nid=0x91`. You convert first, with `printf '%x\n' 145`. Plenty of old how-to guides still say to convert. On JDK 21 or 25, that sends you looking for a thread that isn't there.

**Names get cut short, and Java's IDs mean nothing to the kernel. Join on the TID.**

That's the whole method for a busy thread. `top -H -p <pid>` or `ps -L` gives the TID, and the thread dump gives the Java stack for that TID. The lab builds the join as a small tool. Next, we'll see what happens when a program asks the kernel for more threads than it allows.

try.title: From a hot TID to a Java stack
steps: In the box, start the demo again, and give the fraud scorer a few seconds to burn processor time.
List the threads by processor use, take the top TID, and search the thread dump for it. The `HOT=` line does the copying and pasting for you.
Print the TID in hexadecimal too. That's what you'd search for on JDK 17.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers 120 & pid=$!
sleep 5
ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu,comm | sort -k2 -nr | head -3
HOT=$(ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu --no-headers | sort -k2 -nr | head -1 | awk '{print $1}')
jstack $pid | grep -A3 "nid=$HOT "
printf '%x\n' $HOT
kill $pid

try.expect:
TIDs change on every run:

```text
pid 121 running
  145 99.7 fraud-scorer
  123  0.3 java
  140  0.2 C1 CompilerThre
"fraud-scorer" #27 [145] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=5142.71ms elapsed=5.14s tid=0x0000ffffa014db90 nid=145 runnable  [0x0000ffff753aa000]
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
	at sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers.score(PaymentWorkers.java:45)
	at sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers$$Lambda/0x000007fe01040438.run(Unknown Source)
91
```

One thread uses a whole processor, and the dump names the method: `PaymentWorkers.score`, line 45. `cpu=5142.71ms` after `elapsed=5.14s` says the same thing from the JVM's side: about 5.1 seconds of processor time in 5.1 seconds of life. On JDK 17 the line would say `nid=0x91`.

sections.h: A limit on tasks, and an error that blames memory
sections.body:
A program that calls `fork` in a loop, where every child does the same, is called a fork bomb. It fills the kernel's table of tasks in seconds. Then nothing new can start, not even the shell, the program where you'd type a command to stop it. On one computer shared by many containers, one bad container could do that to all of them. So the kernel can cap the number of tasks for a group of processes.

The groups are **cgroups** (control groups): sets of processes the kernel limits as one unit. Every container is one. (A container is a group of programs that Docker keeps in a box of their own.) Lesson 12, Containers are processes: namespaces and cgroups, takes them apart. The pids controller is the part of cgroups that caps tasks. Docker sets it with `--pids-limit`, and inside the container the limit sits in the file `/sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max`. A thread is a task, so every platform thread counts, along with every thread the JVM starts for itself and every process. In the café, it's a rule about how many baristas fit behind the counter.

When the group is full, `clone` fails with `EAGAIN` ("try again later"), and the JVM throws an error with a misleading name. Here is `ThreadFlood`, a demo that starts platform threads that each wait, like payments waiting on a slow bank. It runs in a container started with `--pids-limit 64`:

```text
[0.322s][warning][os,thread] Failed to start thread "Unknown thread" - pthread_create failed (EAGAIN) for attributes: stacksize: 2040k, guardsize: 4k, detached.
[0.322s][warning][os,thread] Failed to start the native thread for java.lang.Thread "Thread-42"
failed after 42 platform threads: unable to create native thread: possibly out of memory or process/resource limits reached
OS threads in this JVM: 63
```

It got 42 threads. The JVM's own threads used most of the other 22 slots, and the container's shell used one. The error is an `OutOfMemoryError`, Java's error for running out of memory, but the heap was nearly empty: the kernel refused a new task. In the same run, the garbage collector also failed to start a helper thread (`GC Thread#2`), so a full limit hurts the JVM's own work too. The exact number changes from run to run (42 and 50 in two runs here), because the JVM starts helper threads when it needs them.

**An error about native threads points at a task limit. Check the limits before you add memory.**

The usual limits are the cgroup's `pids.max` and the limit on processes per user (`ulimit -u`), which counts threads too. Inside a container, read `/sys/fs/cgroup/pids.events` first: its `max` counter goes up every time a `fork` or `clone` hits the limit. Raising the limit helps for a while. But each platform thread still costs a task and a 2 MB stack while it does nothing but wait. Next, we'll see a way to wait without a task each.

try.title: Hit the pids limit with platform threads
steps: This one runs from the `labs` folder on your Mac, not inside the box: it starts a new container with a limit of 64 tasks.
Predict how many of the 200 platform threads start.
Run it, and read the three parts of the output: the limit, the JVM's complaint, and the `pids.events` counter.

code.title: on your Mac, in labs/
code.src:
docker run --rm --pids-limit 64 -v "$PWD":/labs -w /labs sfz-labbox:1 \
  bash -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max; java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l03/demo/ThreadFlood.java platform 200; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.events'

try.expect:
One run (yours will stop at a slightly different count):

```text
64
[0.300s][warning][os,thread] Failed to start thread "GC Thread#2" - pthread_create failed (EAGAIN) for attributes: stacksize: 2040k, guardsize: 4k, detached.
[0.300s][error  ][gc,task  ] GC(0) Failed to create worker thread
...
[0.322s][warning][os,thread] Failed to start the native thread for java.lang.Thread "Thread-42"
failed after 42 platform threads: unable to create native thread: possibly out of memory or process/resource limits reached
OS threads in this JVM: 63
max 12
```

`pthread_create failed (EAGAIN)` is the kernel refusing a new task. The JVM turns it into an `OutOfMemoryError` while the heap is almost empty. `max 12` in `pids.events` says the group hit its limit 12 times, the garbage collector's failed attempts included. The container is removed when the command ends.

sections.h: Virtual threads: many waits on a few OS threads
sections.body:
Now scale the waiting up: 10,000 payments in flight, each waiting 120 ms on the bank. As platform threads, that's 10,000 tasks, about 20 GB of stack addresses reserved, 10,000 entries against the pids limit, and a kernel juggling 10,000 sleepers. Most of that pays for waiting, and almost none for work.

One way out is to write the program so no thread ever waits. You start each request, hand over a function to run when the answer comes (a callback), and move on. In Java that's `CompletableFuture.thenCompose` and its relatives. It works, but the code turns into chains of callbacks, and when something fails, the error no longer shows the path that led there.

**Virtual threads** have been a finished part of Java since JDK 21 (JEP 444, the proposal that added them). They keep plain code that waits, and move the switching from the kernel into the JVM. Run the same 10,000 waits on them in the same container, and nothing fails:

```text
started 10,000 virtual threads
OS threads in this JVM: 37
```

A virtual thread is a Java object, not a task. To run, it **mounts** on a carrier: an ordinary platform thread from a pool, a `ForkJoinPool`, that the JVM keeps for this job. By default there's one carrier per processor, which is why the demo had 12 `ForkJoinPool-1-worker` threads in a box with 12 processors. Back in the café, the carriers are a few baristas, and the virtual threads are order slips on a rail.

The trick happens when a virtual thread waits, in `Thread.sleep`, a network read, `ReentrantLock.lock()` or `BlockingQueue.take()`. (A lock lets one thread at a time into a piece of code, and `take()` waits for the next item in a queue.) The JVM **unmounts** it. It saves the thread's stack frames, one per method call in progress, on the heap, and frees the carrier, which picks up another virtual thread. When the sleep ends or the data arrives, the virtual thread joins the queue again and mounts on whichever carrier is free. The barista pins the slip back on the rail while the milk steams, and takes the next one. The kernel sees 12 busy tasks. Your code sees 10,000 threads that each wait in plain, top-to-bottom style.

The café picture breaks on what gets put aside. An order slip is a few words, while a virtual thread's slip is its whole stack, copied to the heap and back. And some waits still hold on to the carrier, which is called **pinning**. Up to JDK 23, waiting inside a `synchronized` block pinned. (`synchronized` is Java's built-in way to let only one thread at a time into a block of code.) JEP 491 removed that in JDK 24. Three cases still pin in JDK 25. One is waiting inside a class initializer, a `static {}` block of code that runs once when a class is first used. Another is waiting for another thread to finish setting up a class. The third is waiting in native code, code written in C that called back into Java. A pinned carrier can't run any other virtual thread. So 12 pinned virtual threads can stall every other virtual thread in a JVM with 12 carriers, like baristas stuck holding one cup each.

Virtual threads don't make code faster. JEP 444 says so in as many words: "Virtual threads are not faster threads." They let far more tasks wait at once, without a kernel task each. That suits a program that spends its time waiting on a bank or a database, a program that stores records for others. It does nothing for the busy `fraud-scorer`. Don't keep them in a pool, either. Create one per job. To cap how many call the bank at the same time, use a `Semaphore`, a counter that lets only so many threads past at once.

`jstack` lists platform threads only, carriers included, so the demo's 1,000 virtual threads aren't in it. To see them, use `jcmd`, another tool that comes with Java: `jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json <file>`. Virtual threads remove the cost of waiting. The carriers still need processors, though, and the kernel still decides which task runs on which one, and for how long.

stepper.title: A platform thread, then virtual threads on carriers
stepper.intro: Two carriers, three virtual threads and one platform thread. The TIDs come from the demo program in the lab box.

try.title: Run 10,000 virtual threads under the same limit
steps: Same container settings, same program, but virtual threads, and 50 times as many of them. Predict the number of OS threads.
Run it from the `labs` folder on your Mac.
try.expect:
```text
started 10,000 virtual threads
OS threads in this JVM: 37
```

All 10,000 started and waited at once, on about 37 OS threads: the JVM's usual helpers plus one carrier per processor. The count changes a little between runs (26 and 37 in two runs here), depending on which JIT and garbage collector threads exist at that moment. Every virtual thread waits on a `CountDownLatch`, a gate that opens once, and waiting there unmounts it, so the carriers stay free.

compare.note: Same container, same JDK, same waiting code. Each platform thread is a kernel task with a 2 MB stack reserved, so the limit of 64 tasks stops the program at 42 threads of its own. A virtual thread is an object on the heap that needs a carrier only while it runs, and a thread waiting on a latch unmounts. So 10,000 of them fit on the JVM's usual 37 or so OS threads. The limit didn't change. The number of tasks the program asked the kernel for did.

worked.title: Find the thread that's burning a CPU

steps.say: The payments program sits at 100% of one processor, and payments are slow. First, find which thread uses the processor, from the kernel's side. `ps -L` lists threads with their share of a processor. In the demo, one TID stands out.
steps.code:
ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu,comm | sort -k2 -nr | head -3
#   145 99.7 fraud-scorer
#   123  0.3 java
#   140  0.2 C1 CompilerThre

steps.say: Then ask the JVM what that thread is doing. On JDK 18 and later, search the dump for the TID as it is. `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` prints the same dump if `jstack` isn't installed.
steps.code:
jstack $pid | grep -A3 "nid=145 "
# "fraud-scorer" #27 [145] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=5142.71ms elapsed=5.14s ... nid=145 runnable
#    java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
# 	at sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers.score(PaymentWorkers.java:45)

steps.say: On JDK 17 or older, the dump shows `nid` in hexadecimal. Convert the TID first, then search.

Take two or three dumps a few seconds apart. If the same method is on top every time, that's the loop to look at. If the busy TID belongs to a thread with no `#` number, such as `GC Thread#0` or `C2 CompilerThread0`, the processor time goes to the JVM itself. Heavy garbage collection points to a program that creates objects too fast, and a busy compiler usually calms down once the program has warmed up. If the busy TID isn't in the dump at all, check whether it's the launcher thread (TID = PID), or a thread that native code started.

lab.title: Join the kernel's threads to the JVM's
steps: Open the two captured files. They are real output from this lesson's demo in the lab box: `ps -L -p <pid> -o tid,pcpu,time,comm`, and `jstack <pid>` a moment later.
Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All eight fail.
Write `ThreadDump.nidToTid`: read the text as hexadecimal when it starts with `0x`, and as decimal otherwise.

Write `ThreadDump.parse`. Match each line against `HEADER`, the pattern for a thread's first line. For each header, the thread's own lines run until the next blank line. Take the state from the line that starts with `java.lang.Thread.State:` (first word only), and the top frame from the first line that starts with `at ` (trim the spaces first).
Write the three `ThreadMap` methods. Build a `Map<Int, DumpedThread>` keyed by `osTid` once, and use it in all three.
Run the tests until all eight pass. Then look at what `tasksNotInDump` returns, and say which thread that is.
hints: `HEADER.find(line)` returns null for every line that isn't a thread header, including the dump's date and title lines.
`lines.drop(i + 1).takeWhile { it.isNotBlank() }` gives the lines that belong to the header at index `i`.
The dump also has a thread the ps file doesn't: `Attach Listener`. `jstack` itself made the JVM start it, after `ps` had already run.

drill.title: Hot TID to Java stack, from memory
drill.prompt: Write the commands that take you from "this Java program uses a whole processor" to the Java stack of the thread responsible, on JDK 25. Then write what changes on JDK 17. Check against the answer.

answer.src:
pid=$(pgrep -f ledger-service)                            # or: jcmd -l
ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu,comm | sort -k2 -nr | head -3    # or: top -H -p $pid
jstack $pid | grep -A10 "nid=145 "                       # JDK 18+: nid is decimal

# JDK 17 and older: nid is hex
printf '%x\n' 145                                          # 91
jstack $pid | grep -A10 "nid=0x91 "

recap: Linux runs tasks. A thread is a task made by `clone` with flags that share memory, files and signal handlers. A process is a group of tasks, and its PID is the first task's TID.
Each thread has a folder under `/proc/<pid>/task/`. The kernel keeps only 15 characters of a thread's name, so join the kernel's side and the JVM's side on TIDs, never on names.

A platform thread is one OS thread for life, with about 2 MB of stack reserved on arm64 Linux (1 MB on x86-64). `jstack` shows its TID as `[145]` and `nid=145`; JDK 17 and older print `nid` in hexadecimal.
The pids limit counts threads. When it's reached, `clone` fails with `EAGAIN`, and the JVM throws `OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread` with memory to spare.
Virtual threads mount on a few carriers, one per processor by default, and unmount when they wait. Since JDK 24, `synchronized` doesn't pin; class initializers and native code still do.
The limit: virtual threads make waiting cheap, not work fast. A busy thread still needs a processor, and the kernel still decides who gets one and for how long.
closing:
We started with one barista watching the milk steam while twelve people waited. Threads gave the café's payments program more baristas, each one a task the kernel counts, until a limit of 64 stopped it with an error that blamed memory. Virtual threads put the waiting payments on a rail and let a few baristas work through them.

On a Mac, open Activity Monitor and add the Threads column (View, then Columns). Find your browser, and compare its thread count with the number of processors in your Mac.

Next, we'll watch the kernel share a processor between tasks that all want it, and find out how it decides who runs next.

quiz.q: A payments program runs in a container whose `pids.max` is 512, and it starts a platform thread for every payment. During a busy hour it logs `OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread`, while its heap is 30% used. What happened?
options: The heap filled up with `Thread` objects
The container reached its pids limit, because every platform thread is a task the kernel counts
The JVM ran out of room for the classes it loaded
The computer ran out of processor time
quiz.why: `clone` failed with `EAGAIN` because the group's count of tasks hit `pids.max`, and the JVM reports that as an `OutOfMemoryError`. The heap had room, which is what makes the first option tempting and wrong. `pids.events` would show its `max` counter going up.

quiz.q: `top -H` shows TID 3071 at 100% of a processor, in a program on JDK 21. What do you search for in the `jstack` output?
options: `nid=0xbff`
quiz.why: Since JDK 18, `nid` is printed in decimal, so it matches `top` as it is. `nid=0xbff` is the JDK 17 form, and the old how-to guides that recommend it are the trap. `#` is the Java thread ID, and `tid=` is the address of the JVM's own record for the thread.

quiz.q: A virtual thread asks a database for some rows, and waits while the answer comes over the network. What happens to its carrier on JDK 25?
options: The virtual thread unmounts, and the carrier runs other virtual threads while the answer is on its way
The carrier waits until the answer arrives
The JVM creates a new OS thread for the wait
The request fails, because virtual threads can't wait on the network
quiz.why: Waiting on the network is the case virtual threads were built for. The JVM saves the thread's frames on the heap and frees the carrier. It would stay on the carrier only if it were pinned, for example inside a class initializer. Since JDK 24, a `synchronized` block in the database code no longer pins.

quiz.q: Which of these still pins a virtual thread to its carrier on JDK 25?
options: Waiting on a network read inside a `synchronized` block
Waiting in `ReentrantLock.lock()`
`Thread.sleep(100)`
Waiting inside a class's `static {}` initializer
quiz.why: JEP 491 (JDK 24) stopped `synchronized` from pinning, which is why the first option is the trap for anyone who learned virtual threads on JDK 21. `ReentrantLock` and `sleep` never pinned. Setting up a class still does: a virtual thread that waits in a `static {}` block keeps its carrier until the block finishes.

quiz.q: From Processes: fork, exec, wait and signals: a Java program with 35 threads runs `new ProcessBuilder("pdftotext", "invoice.pdf").start()` to turn a PDF into text. How many threads does the new process have when `pdftotext` starts running?
options: 35, because creating a process copies every thread
One. A new process starts with a single thread, and `execve` gives it `pdftotext`'s program
35 threads, all paused
None until `pdftotext` creates one
quiz.why: `fork` copies only the thread that called it, and Java's own way of starting programs also makes a child with one thread. Then `execve` replaces the program, so `pdftotext` starts with exactly one thread, its main thread, and makes more only if it wants them. The first option is tempting because `fork` copies the memory, and every thread's stack lives in that memory. Only the calling thread comes along as a thread that runs.

flashcards.front: On Linux, what separates a thread from a process?
flashcards.back: Both are tasks made by `clone`. A thread shares memory, files and signal handlers with its group (`CLONE_VM`, `CLONE_FILES`, `CLONE_SIGHAND`, `CLONE_THREAD`). A new process gets copies.

flashcards.front: Where do you list the threads of process 812?
In `"fraud-scorer" #27 [145] ... tid=0x0000ffffa014db90 nid=145`, which number is the OS thread ID?
flashcards.back: 145, shown as `[145]` and `nid=145`. `#27` is the Java thread ID, and `tid=` is an address inside the JVM.

flashcards.front: How does jstack print `nid` on JDK 17, compared with JDK 21?
flashcards.back: JDK 17 prints hexadecimal (`nid=0x91`). JDK 18 and later print decimal (`nid=145`), which matches `top -H` and `ps -L`.

flashcards.front: Why can a JVM fail with "unable to create native thread" while its heap is mostly empty?
flashcards.back: Each platform thread is a kernel task. The cgroup's `pids.max` (or `ulimit -u`) counts them, and `clone` fails with `EAGAIN`.

flashcards.front: What do mount and unmount mean for a virtual thread?
flashcards.back: Mount: run on a carrier, a platform thread. Unmount: when it waits, its frames are saved on the heap, and the carrier runs another virtual thread.

flashcards.front: What still pins a virtual thread in JDK 25?
flashcards.back: Waiting in a class initializer, waiting for another thread to set up a class, and waiting in native code that called back into Java. `synchronized` stopped pinning in JDK 24.

terms.plain: The thing the Linux kernel schedules: a program counter, registers, a stack and an ID. Every thread is a task with its own TID.
The tasks that share one memory, which you know as a process. Its ID is the first task's TID, the PID.
A Java thread that is one OS thread for its whole life.
A Java thread that is an object on the heap, and runs by mounting on a carrier. JDK 21 and later.
A platform thread in the JVM's `ForkJoinPool` that runs virtual threads, one at a time.
A virtual thread that waits but can't unmount, so it keeps its carrier busy.
The native (OS) thread ID in a thread dump. Decimal since JDK 18, hexadecimal before.
The cgroup limit on the number of tasks in a group, threads included, set in `pids.max`.

explain_back.prompt: A friend wants to move the café's payments program from a pool of 200 threads to virtual threads "to make it faster". Explain what virtual threads change at the level of the operating system, and when the move helps.
explain_back.answer: Today each of the 200 threads in the pool is an OS thread. The kernel schedules it, it has a couple of megabytes of stack reserved, and it counts against the container's pids limit. While a thread waits on the bank or the database, its OS thread sleeps and does nothing else. Virtual threads are Java objects. They run by mounting on a handful of carrier threads, about one per processor, and when they wait on the network, the JVM saves their frames on the heap and frees the carrier. So thousands of payments could wait at once on a dozen OS threads. That helps if the payments mostly wait, and the pool's size is what holds them back. It does nothing for work that keeps a processor busy, and no single payment gets any faster. I'd also keep a limit on how many payments call the bank at once, with a semaphore, so we don't flood it. And I'd check that nothing waits inside a class initializer or in native code, which would pin a carrier.

deeper.body:
`jstack` can't show virtual threads, but `jcmd` can write a dump in JSON, a common text format for structured data, that groups every thread by what owns it. For the demo program in the lab box, summarized with a few lines of Python:

```text
$ jcmd $pid Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json
<root>                                                    11 threads
ForkJoinPool-1/jdk.internal.vm.SharedThreadContainer@...  13 threads
java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@133c6e62     1000 threads
```

The 1,000 are the virtual threads from `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`, each marked `"virtual": true`, with an empty name and a stack that ends in `Thread.sleep`. Their `tid` values are Java thread IDs. A virtual thread has no OS thread ID of its own, because it has no OS thread.

The carrier pool's size comes from `jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism`, which defaults to the number of processors the JVM sees. So `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount` and a container's limit on processors both change it, as the Try it showed.

Thread stacks are another reason platform threads cost more than they look. The JVM reserves the whole stack when it creates the thread, about 2 MB on arm64 Linux, plus a guard page. A thread that runs past the end of its stack hits the guard page and fails cleanly, instead of writing into its neighbour's memory. The reservation shows up at once in the process's virtual size (VSZ), the total of the addresses it has set aside. Resident memory (RSS), the real memory in use, grows only as the thread uses its stack, page by page. Lesson 6, Virtual memory: page tables, the TLB and page faults, explains how the kernel does that. Until then, remember that 500 threads reserve about 1 GB of addresses, and may use only a few dozen megabytes of real memory.

JDK 25's thread list also has two names you won't find in a JDK 21 dump. `VirtualThread-unblocker` came with JEP 491 in JDK 24. It finds virtual threads that may carry on after waiting for a `synchronized` block, and hands them back to the scheduler. `ForkJoinPool-1-delayScheduler` is the carrier pool's timer thread. The pool starts it the first time something asks for a delayed task, and in the demo that something was 1,000 sleeping virtual threads waiting for their time to wake.
